findings.summary: The disaster-recovery oracle does not deterministically preserve authoritative provider-native code-host decisions. The accepted Architecture permits a gate decision to be authoritative as an equivalently durable code-host review record instead of a signature record committed to Git, and Gate 1 selects provider-recorded commercial approvals. A12 nevertheless defines the Git/code-host-loss RPO only as zero accepted commits and requires restoration of replicated authoritative refs/objects without enumerating provider-native reviews, statuses, approval records, their durable IDs, identity proof, or server timestamps. A10.1 requires ordinary retrieval after session or hat changes and projection destruction, and A8 governs inventory and lifecycle, but neither requires loss of the primary code-host/control plane followed by restoration and independent verification of every provider-only authoritative record. The Exam can therefore pass disaster recovery with all Git commits restored while an authoritative approval or its provider proof remains lost or unverifiable.
findings.requiredResolution: Amend A12 and the associated A8/A10 evidence contract to enumerate every authoritative code-host record class for each selected binding, including provider-native review, status, and approval records that are not Git commits. Freeze an independent replication or export mechanism and recovery cut; define zero-loss RPO in authoritative decisions and proofs, numeric RTO, stable-ID preservation or a canonical old-to-new mapping, and preservation of subject, active hat, sequence, artifact digest/revision, provider timestamp, and identity/provider proof. Exercise complete primary code-host/control-plane loss plus missing, stale, partial, corrupt, unavailable, and wrong-tenant recovery copies; retain canonical pre/post inventories and hashes and independently verify each restored decision after recovery. Alternatively, require every authoritative decision to have a canonical Git signature record so provider records are evidence rather than sole authority. Any lost or unverifiable authoritative decision must fail.
